tools.name: search_metadata
tools.description:
Structural search for 1C metadata objects by their exact or partial names, categories,
    relationships, and properties.

    Supports two query formats:
    1. **JSON template** (PREFERRED — instant, deterministic, no LLM cost):
       Pass a JSON string with "operation" and parameters, e.g.:
         {"operation": "list_attributes", "object_name": "Контрагенты"}
       Available operations: list_attributes, list_tabular_parts, object_structure,
       list_objects_by_category, list_objects_by_name, list_forms, list_enum_values,
       list_resources, list_dimensions, get_attribute_type, list_attributes_with_type.
       ALWAYS prefer JSON templates when the query maps to a known operation.
    2. **Free-text structural query** — answered from the fulltext and (when
       available) semantic retrieval channels. No Cypher statement is generated
       for it: arbitrary Cypher is not offered by this or any other tool. When
       you need Cypher, use `run_graph_cypher_template`, which runs one of the
       server's allowlisted read-only templates with your arguments as bound
       query parameters and the project scope bound by the server;
       `get_metadata_prompt` lists every template and every JSON operation.

    IMPORTANT: This tool is for STRUCTURAL queries — when you know specific object names,
    categories, or relationship patterns.

    CRITICAL INSTRUCTION FOR LLM:
    - Use object names in Russian WITHOUT category prefix: "Контрагенты", not "Справочник.Контрагенты".
    - When the user asks for attributes/forms/structure of a known object, use JSON template format.
    - For natural language queries, be specific: "реквизиты справочника Контрагенты", not "покажи поля".

    Good queries:
    - {"operation": "list_attributes", "object_name": "Контрагенты"}
    - {"operation": "list_objects_by_category", "category_name": "Документы"}
    - {"operation": "list_objects_by_name", "object_name": "Выпуск", "category": "Документы"}
    - "Где используется справочник Номенклатура"
    - "Формы документа РеализацияТоваровУслуг"

    Parameter naming: handlers tolerate common aliases (e.g. name_pattern → object_name,
    category → category_name, type_pattern → type_name) — но canonical имена надёжнее.
    A parameter naming a concept the operation is not keyed by is REFUSED with an
    error rather than guessed at: `{"operation": "list_attributes_with_type",
    "object": "Документ.Премия"}` asks for attributes whose TYPE is that document.
    For the attributes OF an object use list_attributes with object_name.

    DO NOT use this tool for vague, conceptual, or semantic queries like:
    - "Найди объекты связанные с AI/LLM/нейросетями"
    - "Какие объекты отвечают за продажи"
    For such queries use 'business_search' (semantic search by business descriptions)
    or 'search_metadata_by_description' (search by synonyms, comments, descriptions).

    Args:
        query: JSON template string (preferred) OR structural natural language query
               with specific Russian object names/categories/relationships.
        project_name: Optional configuration name filter. Only needed when multiple configurations are indexed in one database.

    Returns:
        A formatted string with the search results.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: get_metadata_prompt
tools.description:
Get the database description prompt used for generating Cypher queries.
    Returns the system prompt that describes the Neo4j database schema and query examples.
    When template mode is enabled, also includes the list of available template operations,
    and always the allowlisted read-only Cypher templates run by run_graph_cypher_template.

    Returns:
        A string containing the database schema description and Cypher query examples.

Contract parameters (cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: run_graph_cypher_template
tools.description:
Run one of the server's allowlisted read-only Cypher templates.

    Arbitrary Cypher is not available: pass a template id and its arguments
    instead. Call get_metadata_prompt to see the catalogue — every template,
    its description, and the arguments it accepts.

    Args:
        template_id: id of an allowlisted template, e.g. 'object_attributes'.
        arguments: template arguments by name, e.g. {"object_name": "Контрагенты"}.
            Values are passed to Neo4j as query parameters and are never spliced
            into the statement. Arguments named like the project scope are
            refused: the scope of this call is bound by the server.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope with one item per returned row.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: explain_graph_evidence
tools.description:
Show what one node or edge of the graph is grounded in.

    Every answer names the source unit the claim was read from, the coordinates
    inside it (file and line range, or XML property path), the exact hash of
    that source, the extractor version that read it, the assertion type
    (`declared`, `parsed`, `inferred`, `llm`) and a confidence. A relationship
    may hold several independent proofs — declared in XML and exercised by a
    call in BSL — and all of them are returned; none is ever discarded because
    another disagrees with it.

    Args:
        ref: the subject reference of a node or edge, as returned in the
            `subject.ref` field of any evidence answer. Use this to follow an
            edge back to its proof.
        label: node label, e.g. 'MetadataObject' or 'Routine'. Give this with
            `key` instead of `ref` to ask about a node by its identity.
        key: JSON object of the node's identity properties, e.g.
            {"name": "Контрагенты", "category_name": "Справочники",
             "filename": "report.txt"}.
        include_inferred: pass false to exclude heuristic (`inferred`) and
            model-proposed (`llm`) evidence, leaving only what a source states.
        min_confidence: drop evidence below this confidence, 0 to 1.
        include_closed: also return evidence that has been superseded or whose
            source is gone. Off by default: a closed proof explains a past
            answer, not the current graph.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope; `items` holds one evidence record per
        proof, strongest assertion first, and `data` reports whether the
        subject is grounded at all and whether its proofs conflict.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: explain_path
tools.description:
Attach evidence to every step of a path through the graph.

    A path presented as explained while one of its links rests on nothing is
    exactly what this refuses to produce: a step with no proof is returned as
    `grounded: false` and listed in `ungrounded`, so a caller can see which
    link of the chain is unsupported rather than reading the whole path as
    equally reliable.

    Args:
        path: JSON array of subject references, in order — the nodes and edges
            the path traverses. Every evidence answer carries the reference of
            its subject, and a path-finding tool returns them for each step.
        include_inferred: pass false to exclude heuristic (`inferred`) and
            model-proposed (`llm`) evidence from every step.
        min_confidence: drop evidence below this confidence, 0 to 1.
        include_closed: also consider evidence that has been superseded.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope; `items` holds one entry per step with its
        evidence, and `data.complete` says whether every step is grounded.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: find_objects_using_object
tools.description:
Find all metadata objects where the given object is used as a type reference
    in their attributes, dimensions or resources (via USED_IN relationship).

    Use this to answer questions like "Где используется справочник Контрагенты?".

    Args:
        object_name: Name of the metadata object: 'Контрагенты', or with its
                     category prefix to keep only that category —
                     'Справочник.Контрагенты' (also 'Справочники.', 'Catalog.').
        project_name: Optional configuration name filter. Only needed when multiple configurations are indexed in one database.

    Returns:
        Formatted list of objects that reference the given object.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: find_usages_of_object
tools.description:
Find specific attributes, dimensions and resources that reference the given metadata object,
    including their owner object and full type information.

    More detailed than find_objects_using_object: shows each individual attribute/dimension/resource
    that has the object as its type, not just the owner objects.

    Use this to answer questions like "В каких реквизитах используется Контрагенты?".

    Args:
        object_name: Name of the metadata object: 'Валюты', or with its
                     category prefix to keep only that category —
                     'Справочник.Валюты' (also 'Справочники.', 'Catalog.').
        project_name: Optional configuration name filter. Only needed when multiple configurations are indexed in one database.
        limit: Deprecated and ignored. Page with `max_items` and `cursor`, as
               for every tool; accepted only so an older call does not fail.
        offset: Deprecated and ignored, see `limit`.

    Returns:
        Detailed list of attributes/dimensions/resources referencing the object, with owner and type info.
        A long list is paged by the shared contract: a truncated response
        carries a `cursor` for the next page.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: find_register_movement_docs
tools.description:
Find all documents that make movements (проводки / движения) into the given register.

    Use this to answer: "Какие документы делают движения по регистру Продажи?"

    Args:
        register_name: Name of the register: 'Продажи', or with its category
                       prefix to keep only that category —
                       'РегистрНакопления.Продажи'.
        project_name: Optional configuration name filter. Only needed when multiple configurations are indexed in one database.

    Returns:
        List of documents that make movements into the register.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: trace_impact
tools.description:
Recursive impact analysis of a metadata object across the dependency graph.

    Traverses USED_IN, DO_MOVEMENTS_IN and CALLS relationships to answer:
    "If I change this object, what else is affected?" (downstream) or
    "What does this object depend on?" (upstream).

    Args:
        object_name: Exact name of the metadata object (e.g. 'Контрагенты')
        depth: Maximum traversal depth (1-5 for metadata relationships,
            1-10 for CALLS; default 3)
        direction: 'downstream' (who depends on me), 'upstream' (what I
            depend on), or 'both'
        relationship_types: Optional filter — list of relationship types
            to traverse: 'USED_IN', 'DO_MOVEMENTS_IN', 'CALLS'.
            Default: all three.
        project_name: Optional configuration name filter. Only needed when multiple configurations are indexed in one database.
        form_kind: which 1C form model to include among the affected forms —
            'ordinary', 'managed', or 'any' (default, both). A form is affected
            when it belongs to the object or when one of its attributes points
            at it, and each is listed with the model it is.
        response_format: 'text' (default) for the depth-grouped listing, or
            'compact_graph' for the subgraph in compact form — each node
            described once with a stable `id`, each edge a tuple of two
            positions in that node section plus its type. The compact form is
            what the response budget is spent on: it reports `nodes_total`,
            `edges_total` and a `cursor` that continues by periphery, and its
            `id`s can be resolved in full with `fetch_graph_nodes`. It covers
            relations between metadata objects (USED_IN, DO_MOVEMENTS_IN);
            CALLS is a graph of routines and is available in the text form.

    Returns:
        Dependency tree grouped by depth with object names, categories,
        relationship types and traversal paths — or, for 'compact_graph', the
        node and edge sections of the subgraph.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: fetch_graph_nodes
tools.description:
Resolve the stable identifiers of a compact graph back into full nodes.

    A compact graph answer (`trace_impact` with response_format='compact_graph')
    describes each node once and carries an `id` for it. This is how that `id`
    becomes everything the graph holds about the node, so nothing the compact
    form left out is lost — it is one call away.

    Identifiers are scoped: one issued for another project is refused. A
    reference is not an authorisation.

    Args:
        node_ids: JSON array of node identifiers, e.g.
            ["<id from the nodes section>", "<another>"].

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope; `items` holds one record per node that
        still exists, with its label and all its properties, and `data.missing`
        lists the identifiers that matched nothing — an identifier whose node
        is gone is reported, not returned empty.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: resolve_graph_entity
tools.description:
Resolve a reference to one stable node id of this project.

    Takes whatever an agent is actually holding — a UUID out of an export, an
    FQN such as `Справочник.Контрагенты`, a qualified name reaching a routine or
    an attribute, a 1C alias (`Синоним`), or a position in a source file — and
    returns the identifier the rest of the graph tools take.

    When the reference matches more than one node of this project, the answer is
    a typed ambiguity: every candidate, plus the attributes whose values differ
    between them, so the choice can be made without a second call. No "best"
    candidate is picked. A node of another project is never a candidate, not
    even when it is the only match — the same FQN legitimately exists in every
    project of a database, and answering from the wrong one is silent.

    Args:
        reference: the string to resolve. Omit only when source_path and line
            are given instead.
        reference_kind: force one reading — 'uuid', 'fqn', 'qualified_name',
            'alias', 'source_location', 'node_id'. Default 'auto' tries the
            readings the string admits, most precise first, and the first
            reading that matches anything decides the answer.
        entity_kind: restrict to one kind: 'MetadataObject', 'Symbol' (a BSL
            routine), 'Form', 'SourceUnit' (a source file) or 'Chunk'. The
            fastest way to settle an ambiguity that spans kinds.
        source_path: a source file, when resolving a position. 'path:120' in
            `reference` means the same thing.
        line: the 1-based line in that file.
        form_kind: when the reference may name a form, restrict it to one 1C
            model — 'ordinary', 'managed', or 'any' (default). It narrows
            nothing but forms, and every form candidate states its own model.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope. `items` holds the candidates — exactly one
        when the reference resolved — and `data.status` is `resolved`,
        `ambiguous` or `not_found`. `data.resolved.node_id` is the identifier to
        pass on; `data.distinguishing` names the attributes that separate an
        ambiguity's candidates. A candidate that is a form also carries
        `form_kind`.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: explain_graph_entity
tools.description:
Explain one node of the graph: what it is, and what it is connected to.

    Works for every kind of node a search or a traversal hands back —
    `MetadataObject`, a BSL routine (`Symbol`), a `Form`, a source file
    (`SourceUnit`) and an embedded `Chunk` — which is what makes a vector hit or
    a step of an impact path explainable at all.

    Relationships come back grouped by kind and direction, in a fixed order, and
    each group is bounded: a node with thousands of edges of one kind cannot
    crowd the rest of the card out. A group that did not fit reports its full
    `total` and how much is `omitted`, and names the arguments that return it
    whole (`relation_kind`, `direction`, `group_limit`) — so the remainder is
    unrequested, never unreachable.

    Every relationship carries what it rests on: the assertion type, the
    confidence, the evidence id, and the coordinates — a line range in a BSL
    module or a property path in an XML description. An edge nothing grounds is
    returned with `grounded: false` rather than quietly presented as a fact.

    Args:
        reference: what to explain — a node id from `resolve_graph_entity`, or
            any reference that tool accepts. An ambiguous reference returns the
            same typed ambiguity instead of a card for a guessed node.
        reference_kind: force one reading of the reference; see
            `resolve_graph_entity`.
        entity_kind: restrict resolution to one kind of node.
        source_path: a source file, when explaining what is at a position.
        line: the 1-based line in that file.
        relation_kind: return only this relationship type, e.g. 'CALLS',
            'USED_IN', 'HAS_FORM'. This is how an omitted group is read in full.
        direction: 'both' (default), 'outgoing' or 'incoming'.
        group_limit: how many relationships one group may return, up to the
            server's edge limit.
        include_inferred: pass false to drop heuristic (`inferred`) and
            model-proposed (`llm`) proofs, leaving only what a source states.
        min_confidence: drop evidence below this confidence, 0 to 1.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope. `items` holds the relationships in card
        order; `data.card` holds the node, its community and hotspot
        attributes, and the per-group totals with what each group omitted.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: find_graph_path
tools.description:
Explain how two exact entities are connected: the K shortest paths between them.

    Answers "how is A related to B" over the mixed graph — BSL calls, data
    references and metadata structure in one walk — which is a different
    question from the one impact analysis answers. `trace_impact` and
    `trace_call_chain` walk outward from one root; neither takes a second
    entity, and filtering an outward walk down to the paths that happen to
    reach B gives the wrong answer under a budget, because the link joining A
    to B may be one the outward walk dropped when it ran out of room.

    Both endpoints are resolved the way `resolve_graph_entity` resolves them,
    so `from_ref` and `to_ref` take a node id, a UUID, an FQN, a qualified name
    or an alias. An endpoint issued for another project is refused before
    anything is read.

    When there is no path, the answer is an empty result that says how far it
    looked — the depth reached, the nodes examined, and why it stopped — not an
    error. `data.exhaustive` is the field that matters: true means the
    reachable graph was walked to its end and these entities really are not
    connected under these filters; false means the walk stopped at a limit and
    the question is still open.

    Every edge of every returned path carries what it rests on, and each path
    also comes with a `steps` list ready to pass to `explain_path` unchanged.

    Args:
        from_ref: the entity the path starts at.
        to_ref: the entity it must reach.
        direction: 'undirected' (default) walks edges both ways, which is what
            "how are these related" usually means — the edge recording where a
            value came from points the other way. 'directed' follows the arrows.
        edge_types: only walk these relationship types, e.g. ['CALLS',
            'USED_IN']. Omit to walk every type. An allowlist is how a path
            through unrelated link kinds — formally valid, meaningless — is
            avoided.
        max_depth: the longest path to look for, in edges. Capped by the
            server's limit; ask for fewer hops, never more.
        max_paths: how many paths to return, shortest first. Capped the same way.
        include_inferred: pass false to refuse steps that rest only on
            heuristic (`inferred`) or model-proposed (`llm`) proof.
        min_confidence: refuse steps whose strongest proof is below this, 0 to
            1. Narrowing either of these also makes an *unproven* edge
            untraversable: "only what is proven this far" is not met by a link
            resting on nothing.
        form_kind: when an endpoint names a form, which 1C model it is —
            'ordinary', 'managed', or 'any' (default). It settles the ambiguity
            of a name two models share; the walk itself crosses both.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope. `items` holds the paths, shortest first,
        each with its nodes, its edges and their evidence, and a `steps` list
        for `explain_path`. `data.explored` reports the depth reached, the
        nodes examined and the stop reason; `data.exhaustive` says whether an
        empty answer is a conclusion or a budget.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: affected_subgraph
tools.description:
What a change reaches transitively, and the shortest proof of why each thing is in the answer.

    The impact question with its evidence attached. Every affected node comes
    back with a minimal path from the root that reaches it — the whole chain,
    each edge typed and carrying what it rests on — so the claim "this breaks"
    can be checked rather than trusted. `trace_impact` answers the same
    question more cheaply and by level, with one intermediate object in a `via`
    field; use that one when the list is all you need.

    The walk is a true transitive closure, bounded on purpose. When something
    bounds it, `data.exhaustive` goes false and `data.explored.stop_reason`
    names the limit — so an answer that looks small is never quietly a partial
    one.

    Tests are reported separately under `data.related_tests`, each with its own
    root→test path. When the project has no indexed test artifact the status is
    `not_indexed` rather than an empty list: "no tests are indexed" and "this
    change breaks no tests" are different facts. Nothing here runs a test; see
    `get_graph_capabilities` for where execution lives.

    Args:
        roots: the entities that changed, as references `resolve_graph_entity`
            resolves — a node id, a UUID, an FQN, a qualified name or an alias.
            At least one; a root from another project is refused before
            anything is read. If any root fails to resolve the walk does not
            run: an impact answer computed from some of the roots understates
            impact, which is the dangerous direction to be wrong in.
        direction: 'downstream' (default) walks the arrows forwards — what
            depends on the roots, the question "what breaks if I change this".
            'upstream' walks them backwards — what the roots depend on, and the
            direction that finds the tests exercising a routine. 'both' does
            each, costs more, and says less about causality.
        max_depth: how many edges from a root to travel. Capped by the server's
            limit; ask for fewer hops, never more.
        edge_types: only walk these relationship types, e.g. ['CALLS',
            'USED_IN']. Omit to walk every type. An allowlist is how a walk
            through unrelated link kinds — formally valid, meaningless — is
            avoided.
        node_kinds: only report nodes of these kinds or labels, e.g. ['Symbol']
            or ['MetadataObject']. The walk still travels *through* every other
            kind, so the shortest explanation of a reported node may run through
            nodes the filter hides. `related_tests` is unaffected: a test the
            change reaches is reported whatever kinds you asked to read about.
        stop_kinds: stop the walk at nodes of these kinds. Such a node is
            reported, marked `boundary`, and what lies beyond it is not read.
            This is how a change in a common module is analysed without walking
            half the configuration.
        include_inferred: false by default here, unlike elsewhere: impact
            analysis that mixes declared facts with heuristics reports damage
            that is not there. Pass true to include heuristic (`inferred`) and
            model-proposed (`llm`) links.
        min_confidence: refuse steps whose strongest proof is below this, 0 to
            1. On an installation that records evidence, narrowing either filter
            also makes an *unproven* edge untraversable — "only what is proven
            this far" is not met by a link resting on nothing.
        max_nodes: how many distinct nodes the walk may expand. Capped by the
            server's limit.
        max_paths: how many explaining records to return. Records past it were
            still found: `data.total` counts them and `data.omitted` says how
            many are missing.
        form_kind: when a root names a form, which 1C model it is — 'ordinary',
            'managed', or 'any' (default).

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope. `items` holds one record per (root,
        affected node) pair, ordered by depth, root, path and node id, each
        with the node, the explaining path and its evidence. `data.records`
        reports how many records the closure holds, how many this call can page
        through and how many `max_paths` dropped; the envelope's own `returned`
        and `cursor` describe this page of them. `data` also names the roots,
        what bounded the walk, and `related_tests`.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: trace_call_chain
tools.description:
Trace the call chain of a BSL (1C:Enterprise) procedure/function recursively.

    Traverses CALLS relationships in the BSL code graph to build a complete
    call chain from or to a given routine across all metadata objects.

    Use direction="callees" to see what a procedure calls (downstream).
    Use direction="callers" to see what calls a procedure (upstream).

    Four call forms are resolved: a bare call inside one module, a bare call
    to an exported routine of a global common module (`Глобальный = Истина`;
    the edge carries `resolution: global_module`, and `ambiguous: true` when
    several global modules export the name), a common module call
    (`ОбщегоНазначения.Метод()`), and a call through a global metadata
    collection to another object manager module
    (`Документы.РеестрДокументов.ЗаписатьДокумент()`). Resolution is static and
    by name: a call made through a variable, a computed collection name, or any
    other indirection is not resolved and produces no edge, so an empty answer
    here means "no statically resolvable call was recorded", not "this routine
    calls nothing". A routine that runs code named as a string —
    `Выполнить(...)`, `Вычислить(...)` or a library wrapper of them — is marked
    in the tree with its count, and the envelope carries a
    `dynamic_calls_on_chain` warning: the chain past it may be incomplete.
    Read upwards, the answer also lists the scheduled jobs that run the root
    routine (`EXECUTES`) as entry points.

    Examples:
        trace_call_chain(routine_name="ОбработкаПроведения",
                         object_name="РеализацияТоваров",
                         direction="callees", depth=3)
        trace_call_chain(routine_name="ПроверитьКонтрагента",
                         direction="callers")

    Args:
        routine_name: Name of the procedure/function to trace from.
        object_name: Optional owner object name for disambiguation when multiple
            routines share the same name (e.g. 'Контрагенты').
        direction: 'callees' (who does this routine call, downstream) or
            'callers' (who calls this routine, upstream). Default: 'callees'.
        depth: Maximum traversal depth (1-10). Default: 3.
        project_name: Optional configuration name filter for the root routine.
            Only needed when multiple configurations are indexed in one
            database and routines with the same name exist in several of them.

    Returns:
        A call tree grouped by depth with routine names, owner objects,
        module types, directives, signatures and export flags.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: get_object_dossier
tools.description:
Get a comprehensive structural dossier (passport) of a metadata object
    in a single call — deterministic, no LLM.

    Collects all factual information about the object from the graph:
    structure (standard attributes the object really has, attributes,
    tabular parts, dimensions, resources, commands, layouts and — for a
    register — its query virtual tables with parameters), forms, event
    subscriptions, access roles (declared rights of roles), dependencies
    (USED_IN upstream/downstream, register movements), code modules with
    procedure/function signatures, and business description.

    Use this tool as the first step when you need to understand a metadata

tools.name: answer_metadata_question

Answer complex analytical questions about 1C metadata using RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation).

    Use this tool when the question requires REASONING or ANALYSIS across multiple objects,

    - "Какие объекты участвуют в процессе закупки и как они связаны?"
    - "Объясни архитектуру подсистемы управления складом"

    - Object structure → get_object_dossier
    - Find by name → search_metadata
    - Find by meaning → business_search
    - Find code → search_code
    - Dependencies → trace_impact

    Formulate the `question` as a clear, specific Russian-language question.
    Include concrete object names when known (e.g. "Как документ РеализацияТоваровУслуг
    делает движения по регистру Продажи?" instead of "Как работают продажи?").
    The more specific the question, the better the retrieved context and the answer.

    Args:
        question: Analytical question about metadata in Russian. Be specific, include object names when known.
        max_tokens: Maximum tokens for LLM response (default: 4000)
        include_code: Whether to include code snippets in context (default: true)
        project_name: Optional configuration name filter. Only needed when multiple configurations are indexed in one database.

    Returns:

tools.name: search_code
tools.description:
Search BSL (1C:Enterprise) code across all metadata objects using fulltext and/or semantic search.

    When BSL code graph is loaded (LOAD_BSL_SIGNATURES=true), searches individual
    procedures/functions (Routine nodes) for precise results with file/line context.
    Otherwise falls back to searching MetadataObject.program_code.

    CRITICAL INSTRUCTION FOR LLM — choosing search_type and formulating query:
    - **fulltext**: Use when you know the exact procedure/function name or a keyword
      present in the code text. Supports Lucene syntax: AND, OR, wildcards (*), phrases ("...").
      Pass the name or keyword as-is in Russian: "ПроверитьЗаполнение", "Процедура AND Скидк*".
    - **semantic**: Use when searching by PURPOSE or BEHAVIOR, not by name. Rewrite the
      user's question into a description of what the code DOES, in the style of a code comment.
      Example: user asks "где считаются скидки" → pass query="расчет суммы скидки для строк документа продажи"
      because semantic search matches against code descriptions and signatures, not raw text.
    - **hybrid** (default): Combines both. Best for most cases.

    Args:
        query: For fulltext — exact name, keyword, or Lucene expression in Russian.
               For semantic — descriptive phrase about what the code does (rewrite questions into descriptions!).
               For hybrid — can be either; both channels will be tried.
        search_type: "fulltext" (exact matching), "semantic" (by meaning), or "hybrid" (both, default)
        top_k: Maximum number of results per search type (default: 3, so hybrid returns up to 6 total).
               Results are deduplicated by project and module, so `top_k` buys `top_k` distinct
               modules: a common module with many matching procedures contributes one of them
               (CODE_SEARCH_MAX_PER_MODULE) instead of filling the answer. To read more of a
               single module, use the template operations (`list_exported_routines`,
               `get_routine_body`) rather than a larger `top_k`.
        filter_type: Optional metadata category filter (e.g., 'Справочники', 'Документы', 'ОбщиеМодули')
        project_name: Optional configuration name filter. Only needed when multiple configurations are indexed in one database.
        detail_level: Context compression level controlling how much detail is returned per result.
            L0 — full procedure/function code without truncation.
            L1 — signature + description + first 5 callees (default, balanced).
            L2 — brief card: name, owner, module type, export flag, directive.
            L3 — name and score only (minimal tokens, best for large overview lists).

    Returns:
        Search results with code snippets and relevance scores.
        On an installation that builds no embeddings, `search_type="semantic"`
        returns a typed degraded capability naming the structural alternatives,
        and `"hybrid"` is answered through the fulltext channel with a warning
        saying which half is missing.

    Examples:
        search_code("ПроверитьЗаполнение")  # Find function by name (fulltext)
        search_code("расчет суммы скидки для строк документа", search_type="semantic")  # Find by purpose
        search_code("Процедура AND Скидк*", search_type="fulltext")  # Lucene syntax
        search_code("расчет", detail_level="L3", top_k=20)  # Overview list
        search_code("РассчитатьСкидку", detail_level="L0")  # Full code

tools.name: search_metadata_by_description
tools.description:
Search metadata objects by their descriptive fields: name, Синоним (synonym),
    Комментарий (comment), Описание (description), and help_text (Справка).
    Uses Lucene fulltext search across all five fields. When description embeddings
    are available, performs hybrid search (fulltext + vector) with RRF merging.

    Use this tool when the user's question can be answered by matching against
    object names, Russian synonyms, or developer comments — as opposed to
    business_search which matches against generated business descriptions.

    CRITICAL INSTRUCTION FOR LLM:
    1. **Expand the query** with 3-5 synonyms or related 1C terms.
       User asks "зарплата" → pass query="зарплата ЗУП оклад начисления расчет".
    2. **Use Russian terms** — the indexed fields (Синоним, Комментарий, Описание)
       are in Russian. Translate English terms before passing.
    3. **Use filter_type** when the user specifies a category ("справочники про клиентов"
       → filter_type="Справочники", query="клиент контрагент покупатель").
    4. **Use use_fuzzy=true** when the user might have typos or you are unsure
       about the exact spelling.

    Args:
        query: Search keywords in Russian. Expand with synonyms and related 1C terms!
               Lucene syntax supported: AND, OR, "exact phrase", wildcard*.
        top_k: Maximum number of results to return (default: 10)
        filter_type: Optional metadata category filter (e.g., 'Справочники', 'Документы',
                     'РегистрыСведений', 'ОбщиеМодули', 'Перечисления')
        project_name: Optional configuration name filter. Only needed when multiple configurations are indexed in one database.
        use_fuzzy: If true, appends '~' to query terms for fuzzy matching to handle typos (default: False).
        alpha: Weight for fulltext vs vector scores in RRF. 1.0 = fulltext only, 0.0 = vector only, 0.5 = balanced (default: 0.5).

    Returns:
        Ranked search results with relevance scores and description excerpts

tools.name: get_indexing_status
tools.description:
Report the current state of background indexing tasks.

    The server is available from the first second after process start, while
    primary (``structural_indexes``, ``metadata_ingest``,
    ``fulltext_indexes``, ``bsl_code_graph``, ``xml_data_sources``,
    ``form_xml``, ``extension_relationships``) and post-indexing
    (``generate_business_info``, ``vector_indexing``,
    ``routine_embedding_indexing``) tasks run progressively in the
    background. Use this tool to see which data is already available and
    which is still being built — it is the authoritative observability
    surface, because MCP tools themselves do not emit "data is being
    prepared" messages and return empty results while data is unavailable.

    ``source_refresh`` says whether the export has changed since the graph
    was built and what the periodic refresh did about it: the interval, the
    last check, the pending change (counts by kind and a sample of paths),
    why the last tick was skipped (``writer_busy``, ``apply_disabled``), the
    last refresh launched and the last error. A task reported ``completed``
    while ``source_refresh.drift`` is set is a graph that is behind its
    sources.

    Returns:
        A JSON string with one entry per known task: name, status
        (``pending`` / ``running`` / ``completed`` / ``failed`` / ``skipped``),
        optional error, optional start and completion timestamps; plus
        ``source_refresh``.

tools.name: get_access_rights
tools.description:
Declared rights of roles, on an object or on one of its fields.

    What the roles' rights documents declare — not the effective access of a
    user, who may hold several roles. Two kinds of edge, kept apart because the
    configuration keeps them apart: role → object and role → field, each with
    the rights on the edge and the block of the rights document it was read
    from as its proof. On every edge `rights` are the granted rights,
    `denied_rights` the rights set to false explicitly, and a right named in
    neither is not declared by that role. A granted right under a row-level
    restriction (RLS) is listed in `conditional_rights`, and the edge carries
    `conditional: true` and a `restriction_ref`.

    Args:
        role: the role whose rights to return, e.g. 'Бухгалтер'.
        object_name: the object the rights are on. For a field this is the
            object the field belongs to, so "everything this role declares
            on Контрагенты" is one call.
        rights: keep only edges granting at least one of these rights, e.g.
            ['Read', 'Update']. The names are the document's own. An explicit
            denial does not match.
        field_name: keep only edges naming this field. Answers only field
            edges, since an object edge names no field.
        direction: which end you are naming — 'outgoing' asks what a role
            reaches and needs `role`; 'incoming' asks which roles reach an
            object and needs `object_name`; 'both' (default) applies whichever
            filters were given.
        restrictions: 'none' (default) returns the edges. 'conditions'
            returns the RLS condition texts of the matching conditional edges
            instead, one record per restriction headed by its
            `restriction_ref`. 'templates' returns the restriction templates
            of `role` (required) with their texts. Both are paged by
            `max_items` and `cursor`; a text longer than the response budget
            is continued by `cursor`.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope. `items` holds one typed edge per
        declared block, each with its two endpoints, `rights`,
        `denied_rights`, `conditional_rights` when there are any, and the
        evidence it rests on. `data.counts` says how many of each kind came
        back. With restrictions='conditions' or 'templates' the answer is

    declared recorder movements, so an independent information register — one
    with no recorder at all — has no writers by construction, even while two
    documents write it through `РегистрыСведений.X.СоздатьНаборЗаписей()` and a

    functional block that no other tool makes visible.

    finding taken from here can be cited rather than asserted.

            'ПлановыеЕжегодныеОтпуска' or 'Справочник.Номенклатура'. Omit to
            sweep every object that anything reaches — which, with
            `min_referrers`, is the batch form of the question.
        access: 'write' for code that writes a register — a record-set factory
            call or a document posting through `Движения.X` — 'read' for a
            table named as a source in query text. Omit for both.

        referrers each target has, and every edge carries its evidence. A

    recognised from the record-set factory call or the movement collection,

        attribute_name: keep only links through an attribute of this name.
        depth: how many hops of the data path to walk. 1 (default) is the
            object's own links; more follows the chain outward.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope; `items` holds the typed `USED_IN` edges
        with their evidence, and `data.reached` names the objects each hop
        arrived at.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: get_report_dcs_lineage
tools.description:
Report → data composition schema → data sets and their queries → fields.

    The whole chain a report's data travels, as typed edges: the schema the
    report owns, the data sets it declares and the query each runs, the fields
    every set supplies, and the parameters, calculated fields, groupings,
    filters and templates the schema exposes. Every link carries the XML path
    of the element it was read at, so any step can be opened in the document.

    Creating, editing or validating a composition schema is not served here and
    never will be: this server reads sources and changes nothing. Ask
    `get_graph_capabilities` for 'create_dcs', 'edit_dcs' or 'validate_dcs' and
    it answers with the typed delegation to EDT MCP.

    Args:
        report: the report whose lineage to return.
        layout: one composition schema of it, when the report has several.
        data_set: keep only this data set and the fields it supplies.
        depth: 1 stops at report → schema; 2 adds the data sets and their
            queries; 3 (default) adds fields, parameters, groupings, filters
            and templates.
        stages: read only these stages — any of 'schema', 'data_set', 'field',
            'parameter', 'grouping', 'filter', 'template'. A stage below the
            requested depth is not read even when named.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope; `items` holds the typed edges of the
        chain, each with its XML-path evidence, and `data.counts` how many
        links of each stage came back.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: compare_base_and_extension
tools.description:
Compare a base metadata object with its extension counterpart.
    Shows structural differences: which attributes, forms, and routines
    were added by the extension, which were overridden, and which remain unchanged.

    Requires the base configuration and the extension to be loaded into the same Neo4j database
    (with different PROJECT_NAME values) and extension relationships to be built.

    Args:
        object_name: Name of the metadata object (e.g. "Контрагенты"). A type
            prefix names its category ("Документ.РеестрДокументов"). A bare
            name that objects of two categories of the extension share compares
            the alphabetically first category, names it in the heading and
            lists the other qualified names.
        extension_name: Name of the extension (value of EXTENSION_NAME used during loading)

    Returns:
        Detailed comparison report or an error message if the object is not found.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: resolve_effective_entity
tools.description:
Resolve an entity across the extension layers: which version runs, and which
    no longer does.

    In a configuration with several extensions the same routine can exist in
    the base configuration and in every extension over it. Which one the
    platform runs is decided by the order the extensions apply in
    (EXTENSION_APPLY_ORDER, declared per extension at ingestion) and by what the
    extension declares it does — `&Вместо` and `&ИзменениеИКонтроль` put the
    base version out of use, `&Перед` and `&После` leave it running alongside.

    The anchor may be named in any layer: asking about the base routine and
    asking about the extension routine that overrides it return the same
    answer.

    Args:
        object_name: the metadata object the entity belongs to (its own name
            when entity_kind is 'MetadataObject'), e.g. "Контрагенты".
        entity_kind: 'MetadataObject' (default), 'Routine', 'Form' or 'Module'.
        entity_name: name of the routine, form or module; required for those
            kinds and ignored for 'MetadataObject'.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope. Each item holds `effective` (the version
        that runs, with its layer), `superseded` (versions replaced by a later
        layer, each naming the layer that supersedes it), `wrapping` (versions
        that run in addition to the effective one) and `extending` (extension
        objects that add to a base object rather than replace it). `data.layers`
        lists the layers of this project in application order.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: compare_graph_scope
tools.description:
What changed between two states of the graph: two generations, two projects,
    or an extension and the base configuration it borrows from.

    One comparison per call, chosen by which argument names the other side.
    Naming two of them is refused rather than resolved by precedence.

    * `base_generation` — what a re-index did to this project. The state
      compared *to* is the active generation unless `target_generation` names
      another. A generation still in the graph (the active one, or one built and
      not yet promoted) is compared with its properties; an older one exists
      only in the evidence, which keeps closed proofs for the retention window,
      so the comparison is by source hash and every difference still carries its
      proof.
    * `compare_project_id` — another project of this installation, named
      explicitly. The response returns both sides with their namespace and
      project; nothing is ever compared across projects implicitly.
    * `extension_ref` — one extension's entities against the base entities they
      borrow or replace, paired by the graph's own EXTENDS/OVERRIDES edges, so an
      override named differently from what it overrides is still recognised as
      its version. Each difference names the layer it comes from and, where the
      source states one, what the override does to the base version.

    Only differences are returned. Unchanged entities are counted, never listed.
    Every difference carries stable IDs and, when evidence records them, the
    before and after source hashes — which is what tells a real change from a
    re-index that happened to rewrite the same facts (`evidence_only`).

    Args:
        base_generation: the generation to compare from.
        target_generation: the generation to compare to; defaults to the active
            one.
        compare_project_id: another project to compare this one against.
        extension_ref: the extension layer to compare against the base
            configuration.
        node_kinds: restrict the comparison to these node kinds, by entity kind
            ('MetadataObject', 'Symbol', …) or by graph label ('Routine',
            'Form', …). Omit to compare every kind — and narrow it when a kind
            is too large to be read whole.
        edge_types: restrict relationship differences to these types, e.g.
            ['CALLS', 'USED_IN']. Omit for every type.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope. `items` holds the differences, grouped by
        entity kind and operation in that order; `data.summary` counts them for
        nodes, properties, relationships and evidence; `data.base` and
        `data.target` say exactly which two states were compared. When the two
        states were built by different extractor versions,
        `data.incompatibility` says so and no differences are computed.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: list_graph_projects
tools.description:
List the graph projects registered in this MCP installation.

    Only projects of this installation's ``MCP_NAMESPACE`` are returned: one
    Neo4j database may serve several MCP installations, and each one sees its
    own projects only.

    Returns:
        A JSON string with ``mcp_namespace`` and one entry per project:
        identifier, configuration root, mode, lifecycle status, whether it
        currently serves project-data tools, its active and staging
        generations, ingestion state, and last error.

Contract parameters (cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: get_graph_project_status
tools.description:
Report the lifecycle and ingestion status of one registered project.

    Answers three questions separately, because a single "healthy" flag hides
    the state that matters during a rebuild: whether this process is alive,
    whether Neo4j and each retrieval lane (exact / fulltext / vector / hybrid /
    traversal) are ready, and how far the current ingestion has got.

    Progress is computed from processed bytes of the project's file manifest,
    not from the number of files: on a 1C export file sizes differ by orders of
    magnitude, and a file-count percentage stalls on large modules. Values are
    monotonic and never exceed 100%; when sizes are unknown, progress is
    reported as unknown rather than as a number that looks meaningful.

    Args:
        project_id: identifier of a project registered in this namespace.
        operation_id: optional identifier of an administrative operation
            (``register`` / ``refresh`` / ``delete``). When given, its recorded
            result is included, so a client that lost the original response can
            find out what happened without re-issuing the operation. An
            unrecorded id is reported as ``known: false``, not as an error.
        generation: optional generation to pin the report to. Must be the
            project's active or staging generation.

    Returns:
        A JSON string with the project's registry status, active and staging
        generations, ingestion state (``never_run`` / ``running`` / ``idle`` /
        ``failed``) with per-phase records, byte-based progress with a smoothed
        ETA, checkpoint counters, liveness, per-lane readiness, and the last
        error as a correlation ID plus error type — the full error text is
        written to the server log under the same correlation ID.
        When staging validation is switched on, a ``validation`` report of the
        most recent generation is included: counts per entity and edge type,
        and the invariants a refused generation violated with their expected
        and observed values. That is the answer to "the refresh finished and
        the graph did not change".
        Only this project is described; no other project's ingestion is
        disclosed.

Contract parameters (cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: register_graph_project
tools.description:
Register a graph project in this namespace (admin profile only).

    A newly registered project holds no data and does not yet serve
    project-data tools: call ``refresh_graph_project`` to build and promote its
    first generation.

    Args:
        project_id: identifier callers will pass to project-data tools.
        configuration_root: root of the 1C configuration export feeding it.
        operation_id: caller-chosen identifier making the call idempotent —
            repeating it returns the first result instead of registering twice.
        mode: ingestion/serving mode of the project.

    Returns:
        A JSON string with the resulting project status, or an ``error``
        object with a typed ``code``.

Contract parameters (cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: refresh_graph_project
tools.description:
Rebuild a project into a new generation and promote it (admin profile only).

    A generation is published only on success, so a failed refresh promotes
    nothing and records nothing as done — repeating it re-derives and finishes
    the same plan. It is not a rollback: the lanes apply the plan to the live
    project graph unit by unit, so a refresh that fails partway leaves what it
    already wrote in place, and says which lanes those were in
    ``error.live_mutation`` (or ``applied_lanes`` when the failure is typed).

    ``incremental`` goes through one contract: the project's source unit
    manifest is built, an add/change/delete plan is derived from it, the graph,
    fulltext and vector lanes are driven from that same plan, and a new
    generation is published only after all of them have been verified. A
    per-file refresh is the same pipeline with fewer entries, never a separate
    fast path.

    Those lanes update the live graph one source unit at a time, and only BSL
    modules have a per-unit update. A plan naming other kinds — metadata
    descriptors, forms, roles, subscriptions — is therefore refused **before
    anything is written**, with ``refresh_capability_unavailable`` naming the
    kinds and pointing at ``mode=full``. The same refusal covers the embedding
    contour: an installation that builds embeddings must be able to rebuild the
    ones a refresh invalidates, so it is refused before the first vector is
    cleared when it cannot.

    ``full`` is the other pipeline, and it is the one that makes a newly
    registered project accessible: the project-scoped ingestion pipeline reads
    the registered ``configuration_root`` into a disposable staging generation,
    the staging assertions run against it, and promotion swaps it onto the
    project in one transaction. Nothing of the live project changes until that
    swap. Reading a whole configuration takes minutes to hours, so the call
    answers ``accepted`` with the ``staging_generation`` as soon as the
    rebuild is set up, and the rebuild runs on in the server: poll
    ``get_graph_project_status(project_id, operation_id=...)``, whose
    ``operation.status`` reads ``accepted`` while it runs and ``completed``
    once the generation is promoted. A rebuild that fails leaves the project
    in ``ingestion_state=failed`` with ``last_error`` and frees the
    ``operation_id`` for a retry.

    That staging generation is a second ``project_id``, which exists only under
    ``GRAPH_SCOPE_ENFORCED``. Without it there is nothing to build into and
    nothing to promote, so the rebuild is refused with
    ``data_store_unavailable`` before its first statement rather than writing
    into the live project on the way to a promotion that cannot run.

    A full rebuild also builds only what the ingestion pipeline builds: the
    structural graph, the BSL code graph, the XML data sources and the forms.
    The business descriptions and every embedding contour are made afterwards,
    by lanes a rebuild does not run — and promotion *deletes* the active
    generation's data. So a project that already holds them is refused with
    ``refresh_capability_unavailable`` before anything is written, and told to
    refresh through the source unit manifest instead. When it holds none, the
    answer names the contours the new generation does not carry in
    ``lanes_not_built``.

    An installation without the source unit manifest has no incremental
    pipeline at all, and does not pretend to one: ``mode=incremental`` there
    rebuilds the whole project, and the answer says so — ``mode`` is ``full``
    and ``requested_mode`` carries what was asked. ``changed_paths`` is refused
    on that installation rather than accepted and ignored.

    Args:
        project_id: identifier of a project registered in this namespace.
        operation_id: caller-chosen identifier making the call idempotent —
            repeating it returns the first call's handle and creates no second
            generation, whether that call has finished or is still running.
        mode: ``incremental`` (default) applies only what changed since the
            last promoted generation, and only for the kinds the per-unit lanes
            can apply; ``full`` rebuilds the whole project from its registered
            root and promotes the result.
        changed_paths: optional list of source unit paths to narrow an
            incremental refresh to. Units left out keep their previous manifest
            record, so a change that was not applied stays pending rather than
            being recorded as done.
        expected_generation: optional generation the caller believes is active.
            When it is not, the refresh is refused with ``stale_generation``
            instead of being applied to a generation the caller did not mean.

    Returns:
        A JSON string with the operation handle (``operation_id`` and
        ``status``: ``accepted`` while the work runs, ``completed`` once it
        has), the promoted generation when one was published, the plan's
        counts and reason codes, per-lane results and the run's metrics — or an
        ``error`` object with a typed ``code``.

Contract parameters (cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: refresh_extension_layers
tools.description:
Re-read the extension layers of this installation (admin profile only).

    What the startup catalog phase cannot do. That phase brings the graph in
    line with the *catalog* — it adds layers whose export appeared and removes
    layers whose export is gone — but a layer that is already in the graph comes
    back ``untouched``, because nothing tells it which exports changed. And a
    list of changed layers would not be enough on its own: the metadata, BSL and
    form lanes each resume over what the graph already holds, so a re-exported
    patch under an unchanged path stays as it was.

    This call forces the re-read. Each named layer's metadata objects, BSL
    modules and form structures are read from its export again and merged over
    what is there; nothing is cleared, so a layer that has not really changed
    converges to the state it already had, and a layer whose export moved on
    replaces its own entities and no one else's.

    Confined to the layers of this installation's base project, one layer
    identity at a time. The base configuration is not a layer of the catalog and
    is never re-read by this call; neither is any other project's layer.

    This is a pass over the catalog, so it also keeps that pass's ordinary
    reconciliation: a layer in the graph whose export is gone from the catalog is
    removed, as the startup phase would remove it, and `EXTENSION_CATALOG_SYNC=false`
    still turns that off. Naming layers narrows what is re-read, not what is
    reconciled.

    Single-writer, like every rebuild here: the call is refused with
    ``ingestion_busy`` while this process's own indexing is still writing, and
    with ``refresh_in_progress`` while another pass over the same project runs.
    Both are decided before the first write, so a refusal costs nothing.

    A pass reads exports and takes as long as that takes — expect a long call.
    One layer that fails does not stop the rest: it is named in ``failed`` and is
    not counted in ``refreshed``. Every attempted layer failing is a
    misconfiguration rather than a bad export, and answers ``operation_failed``.

    Args:
        operation_id: caller-chosen identifier making the call idempotent —
            repeating it returns the first result instead of re-reading the
            layers twice. A failed pass is not recorded, so the same identifier
            may be retried.
        layers: extension layer names to re-read. Omit it to re-read every layer
            the catalog holds. A name the catalog does not hold is reported in
            ``warnings`` and refreshes nothing — it never widens the pass.

    Returns:
        A JSON string naming the base project and catalog, the layers actually
        re-read, the ones that failed, the pass's per-action counts and its
        warnings — or an ``error`` object with a typed ``code``.

Contract parameters (cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: delete_graph_project
tools.description:
Delete a project's graph data and its registration (admin profile only).

    Deletion is confined to this ``mcp_namespace + project_id``: counts,
    checksums, and generations of the other projects in the database are
    unaffected.

    Args:
        project_id: identifier of a project registered in this namespace.
        operation_id: caller-chosen identifier making the call idempotent —
            repeating it returns the first result instead of deleting twice.

    Returns:
        A JSON string with how many entities were deleted, or an ``error``
        object with a typed ``code``.

Contract parameters (cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: list_graph_capabilities
tools.description:
List every published tool with its version and hash, the feature gates this
    installation runs under, and the hard limits every response is bounded by.

    The answer to "what can I call here, and under what rules" in one call.
    Each item names a tool, the version of its own contract, a hash of the shape
    it currently publishes, whether it takes the project scope, and its
    read-only / idempotent / destructive annotations. `data` carries the shared
    contract version, the feature gates and the limits.

    A feature gate is not a capability: the tool exists either way. What a gate
    decides is how its answer should be *read* — whether it is isolated by
    project, grounded in evidence, checked before promotion. `data.limits` is
    the rest of what the envelope does not already state: walk depth, fan-out,
    call timeout.

    Distinct from `get_graph_capabilities`, which answers a different question:
    that one draws the boundary between what this server analyses and which
    executions it delegates to another service. This one describes the surface.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope; `items` holds one entry per published
        tool in name order, `data` the contract version, profile, feature gates
        and limits.

Contract parameters (cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: get_graph_tool_schema
tools.description:
Return the JSON Schema, annotations, version, hash and a compact example of
    one published tool — or of all of them.

    The example is not decoration. A JSON Schema says what is *accepted*; only a
    worked call says what a real one looks like, and an agent that has to infer
    it from types infers it wrongly for exactly the arguments that matter — the
    qualified names of this domain.

    The schema returned is the one the server publishes in `tools/list`, derived
    from the same function. A parity test fails the build when a published tool
    has no documented entry here, and when an entry names a tool that is not
    declared, so this cannot drift into describing a surface that no longer
    exists.

    Args:
        tool: a published tool name. Omit it for every tool.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope; `items` holds one entry per described
        tool with `input_schema`, `annotations`, `version`, `hash`, `summary`
        and `example`.

    Raises:
        invalid_argument: for a name this server does not publish. An empty
            answer would be indistinguishable from a tool that has no schema.

Contract parameters (cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: list_plugins
tools.description:
Report every plugin file this server loaded, and what each of them declares.

    The answer to "what is this server actually running", which a client cannot
    get from `tools/list`: a plugin changes what published tools do without
    changing their names. Each item is one file, with the hooks and tables it
    declares, the classification of each hook (`call-scoped` affects one call;
    `derived-state` shapes the graph, fulltext and vector state and its source
    is part of the fingerprint those are rebuilt against), whether each hook is
    enabled, the error that disabled it, how many times it failed, the time
    accumulated in it, and a digest of the file's source.

    `data` carries the order the files run in — sorted by file name, and each
    hook is a pipeline in that order — the current plugin epoch, the files that
    refused to load with the reason each gave, the declared aliases and tool
    presets, the build counters of the last ingestion, and the two settings that
    govern failures.

    Args:
        project_id: a project registered in this namespace. Only used to check
            whether the aliases plugins declared resolve to anything: without
            it, every alias is reported with `resolved: null`, which means "not
            checked here" rather than "resolves to nothing".

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope; `items` holds one entry per loaded plugin
        file in the order they run, `data` the epoch and the rest of the state.

Contract parameters (cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: reload_plugins
tools.description:
Re-read the plugin directory and put the whole set in force (admin profile only).

    Every file is read again and the set is replaced atomically at a new plugin
    epoch. A directory in which one file no longer loads changes nothing at all:
    the previously loaded set stays in force and the answer names the file and
    the reason it refused. Half a new set is a state nobody asked for.

    Call-scoped hooks take effect on the next call. Derived-state hooks take
    effect at the *next build*, never retroactively — the graph, the fulltext
    index and the vectors already stored were shaped by the hooks that were
    loaded when they were built, and rewriting that claim without rebuilding
    would make the state describe rules it was not produced under.

    A new epoch invalidates outstanding continuation cursors: a client paging
    through an answer is refused with `stale_plugin_epoch` and repeats the call
    rather than paging into a differently shaped answer.

    Args:
        operation_id: caller-chosen identifier making the call idempotent —
            repeating it returns the first call's result instead of starting a
            second epoch. A reload that changed nothing because a file refused
            to load is not recorded, so the same id may be retried once the file
            is fixed.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope; `data` carries whether the set was
        replaced, the new epoch, the order the files run in, and the files that
        failed with their reasons.

Contract parameters (cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: get_graph_schema
tools.description:
Report the node kinds and edge kinds this project's graph holds.

    Two halves with two different authorities. The node kinds are declared by
    this server — every label it writes, with the properties its identity is
    keyed by — and each is marked `present` or not for this project, so an empty
    kind is visibly empty rather than missing. The edge kinds can only come from
    the graph: a relationship type is written between whatever the extractors
    found, and which pairs of labels it actually connects is a fact about the
    data, not a declaration.

    Only this project's kinds are reported. Which kinds a neighbouring project
    holds is not disclosed, and neither is its existence.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope; `items` holds the node kinds followed by
        the edge kinds, each tagged with `kind` ('node' or 'edge') — one list,
        so a truncated answer pages both halves together. `data` counts them
        rather than repeating them.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: get_graph_stats
tools.description:
Count this project's graph by node type, edge type, evidence type and
    confidence.

    Four breakdowns rather than one total, because a total cannot show a
    lopsided extraction: a configuration whose forms loaded and whose modules
    did not has a healthy object count and no routines, and only the per-type
    numbers say so. Evidence is counted by assertion type and by confidence
    bucket for the same reason — a graph resting mostly on inference is a
    different graph from one resting on what the sources declare.

    An empty graph is a valid state. It returns zeros with `data.empty` set,
    never an error: a project that has been registered and not yet built is
    exactly the case an operator asks about.

    With GRAPH_SCOPE_ENFORCED on, the counts are confined to this project and
    to the generation currently serving it, which the response context names;
    no other project's counts are included. With it off they count the whole
    database, and `data.scope_confined` is false. Evidence and confidence
    counts are zero by design while the installation records no evidence
    (`data.evidence_recorded` false, REFERENCE_EVIDENCE_ENABLED off); whether
    the graph holds data is `data.empty`.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope; `items` holds the per-node-type counts,
        and `data` the other three breakdowns — `edges`, `evidence`,
        `confidence` — with the totals, `empty`, `scope_confined` and
        `evidence_recorded`. The node counts are not
        repeated in `data`: `items` is what the shared cursor pages, and a whole
        copy beside a paged one would eventually disagree with it.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: list_graph_indexes
tools.description:
List the indexes this database holds, with their state, population and the
    share of this project's nodes each one covers.

    Population and coverage answer different questions and both are needed.
    Population is what the *server* has built — an index that exists and is 40%
    populated answers 40% of the queries it is for. Coverage is what share of
    this project's nodes of that label actually carry the indexed property: a
    fully built index over a property nine tenths of the project does not have
    is a healthy index with a tenth of the reach, and only the second number
    says so.

    Indexes are one schema of the whole database and their keys carry the
    composite project scope rather than their names, so the list itself
    discloses no project. The coverage is counted inside this project only.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope; `items` holds one entry per index with
        `type`, `entity_type`, `state`, `population_percent`, `coverage`, the
        labels and the properties. `data` counts how many are online.

Contract parameters (project_id, generation, cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: health_graph
tools.description:
Report server liveness, Neo4j availability, provider availability and
    per-lane readiness — each of them separately.

    A single "healthy" flag makes a cold start undiagnosable, because four
    independent things are being asked about at once:

    * `liveness.process` — this process answers. Deliberately not conditioned on
      anything else: a live server with a dead database is a different situation
      from a dead server, and one flag cannot say which.
    * `neo4j.available` — whether the database answered a trivial statement.
    * `providers.embedding` / `providers.chat` — each with its own state.
      "No API key" and "switched off by graph-only mode" call for different
      action and are never merged.
    * `readiness.lanes` — exact, fulltext, vector, hybrid and traversal, each
      reported on its own. A ready structural graph with an unbuilt vector lane
      is a working truncated service, which `readiness.state` names
      `ready_structural` rather than calling it a failed start.

tools.name: unpack_ordinary_form
tools.description:
Read one standalone ordinary-form `Form.bin` into an editable workspace.

    An ordinary form (обычная форма) is exported as a binary container, unlike
    a managed form's `Ext/Form.xml`. Do not edit `Form.bin` directly and do not
    read it as XML: unpack it here, edit the payload, and build it back with
    `build_ordinary_form`.

    The workspace holds `payload/` — the container's entries verbatim, and the
    only thing a rebuild reads — plus `decoded/`, derived views for reading
    (`form.json`, the layout as JSON-compatible data; `module.bsl`, the form
    module). Editing a derived view is refused by the build rather than
    silently dropped.

    What the layout can say: the brace tree is positional. It is structurally
    parseable and it names no elements. Named element trees (`*.elem.json`)
    come only from high-level extraction of a whole CF/CFE/EPF, where the
    surrounding metadata supplies the names. Nothing here is invented.

    Args:
        form_path: the `Form.bin` to read. Absolute path; Cyrillic is normal.
        workspace_path: where to materialise the workspace. Must be new, empty,
            or a workspace this tool wrote (then `overwrite` is required).
            A non-empty directory this tool did not write is always refused.
        overwrite: replace an existing workspace of this contract.
        include: `summary` (default, paths only), `structure`, `module` or
            `all` — which bounded preview to embed in the answer.
        max_chars: bound on each embedded preview. Clamped to the server's cap.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope; `data` carries the `ordinary-form/1`
        payload: `status`, `entries` (name, kind, size, sha256, encoding, and
        the paths of payload and decoded view), `source`, `manifest_path`, and
        the previews asked for. A refusal arrives as `status="error"` with
        `error_code` and an actionable `hint`.

Contract parameters (cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.

tools.name: build_ordinary_form
tools.description:
Write an ordinary-form workspace back to a `Form.bin`, and verify it.

    Verification re-reads what was just written, with the same code that reads
    the original, and compares the *logical payload* — entry names, sizes and
    SHA-256 of the payload bytes. It deliberately does not compare the final
    binaries: the container records carry write timestamps, so a rebuilt
    `Form.bin` differs byte for byte from its source even when nothing changed.
    `binary_identical` reports that fact; `verification.status` is what says
    whether the form survived.

    Args:
        workspace_path: a workspace written by `unpack_ordinary_form`.
        output_path: the `Form.bin` to write. Never replaced silently.
        overwrite: replace an existing output file.
        verify: re-read the result and compare the payload. Leave it on.

    Returns:
        The shared response envelope; `data` carries `output` (path, size,
        sha256), `source` (the original recorded at unpack time),
        `binary_identical`, `verified`, `verification` (`match` / `mismatch` /
        `skipped`, with per-entry hashes) and `changed_entries` — the payload
        entries edited since the unpack.

Contract parameters (cursor, max_items) and the response envelope: see the server instructions or get_graph_tool_schema.
